title: Written down
hook: in the first century BCE the Pali canon was written on palm leaves at Aluvihara

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sanghamitta: a branch in a golden vessel, a king wading into the sea. Your line was it still grows. Did you water something living? Day eight hundred sixty-three.

A strip of dried palm leaf, long and narrow, lies across a monk's knee. He holds a metal stylus and scratches letters into its surface, line after careful line. Later, soot and oil will be rubbed across the leaf and wiped away, and the dark will stay only in the scratches, so the words appear. A whole library can be made this way, one leaf at a time, tied between wooden boards. In Sri Lanka, the chronicle says, there came a day when the monks decided the teaching had to be written down in books.
screen: `A STRIP OF PALM LEAF.` → `A STYLUS SCRATCHES LETTERS.` → `THE MONKS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: First, a teaching that lived in voices. Earlier in these weeks we heard how the teaching was carried by memory: monks learned the discourses and the rules by heart, and chanted them together, so a mistake by one could be caught by the others. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say that the three baskets of the teaching, and the commentaries on them, had been handed down that way, by mouth. Second, the fear. The Mahavamsa sets this moment in the reign of King Vattagamani, a troubled reign, in which the king himself is driven from his throne for a time. The chronicle says the monks saw that people were falling away, and they came together and wrote the texts down in books, so that the true teaching might endure. That's the whole reason it gives. Not convenience. Survival. Third, the place. Tradition names the spot as Aluvihara, a monastery among great rocks, where the work is said to have been done. Pilgrims still visit it. Fourth, what changed and what didn't. Writing didn't end the chanting. Monks still learn texts by heart and recite them together, and in monasteries today the voice is still one way the teaching is received. But from then on there was a second keeper, a quieter one: leaves in a bundle, waiting for anyone who could read. When a manuscript wore out, it could be copied fresh. That's the old way a text stays alive, the way a tree does: not by never changing, but by being renewed. The monks at Aluvihara didn't know who would read their leaves. They wrote for strangers, so the teaching wouldn't depend on any one memory, or any one life.
screen: `A TEACHING THAT LIVED IN VOICES.` · `AFRAID IT COULD BE LOST.` · `WRITTEN AT ALUVIHARA.` · `CHANTING GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one line. Find paper and a pen if you can, or a note on your phone if you can't. Choose one line that matters to you: something from these lessons, a saying from someone you love, a line from a text of your own tradition. Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk scratched each letter into the leaf. Read it back once. Then put the pen down, settle, and let the line rest with you while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Written down. The moment, as the chronicle tells it, when the teaching carried by voices was set down in books, so it would endure. Today's word.
Your line: on palm leaves. Today, keep the line you wrote somewhere you'll see it again, and read it once more before you sleep. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Theravada monasteries keep both ways alive: monks memorize and chant the texts together, and the written canon, once kept on palm leaves, is now printed and studied as well.

original.note: Pali: pitaka, a basket. the canon is called the three baskets.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone sat down one day and wrote the Buddhist bible.
what it means: in the chronicle, texts long kept by memory were written in books, so they wouldn't be lost in hard times.
what a scholar hears: the Mahavamsa gives the reason in a few lines and sets it in Vattagamani's reign; the name Aluvihara comes from tradition, and chanting carried on beside the written page.
recall: told the lay people not to give

sources.ref: Mahavamsa 33 (the reign of Vattagamani; the texts written in books)

notes: The outline hook gives 'the first century BCE'; the chronicle names the reign, not a century, so the script leaves the date out (claims rule). A Keeper may want the scholarly dating added with attribution.
The Mahavamsa does not name Aluvihara; the script attributes the place to tradition. Confirm.
Palm-leaf technique (stylus incision, blackening with soot and oil) described generally; confirm.
'Driven from his throne for a time' summarizes Vattagamani's exile in Mahavamsa 33; confirm.
Trapdoor floor 1 uses 'the Buddhist bible' as the common misreading; change if a Keeper finds it unfair.
Editor: 'a few days ago' corrected (day 852 is eleven days back).

Audit: the hook implied the chronicle describes palm-leaf writing; Mahavamsa 33 says only that the texts were written 'in books', so the hook's last line now says that, and the palm-leaf picture stays a general description.
